name: French
intro: Learn broadly standard contemporary French and then widen exposure to France, Belgium, Switzerland, Quebec and other Francophone communities. Vocabulary, speech rhythm and conventions vary. Keep gender and plural with nouns, and learn verbs with their prepositions. Formal written French and spontaneous speech differ markedly. The long-form foundation courses support elementary drills; the units here explain the path into advanced argument and style.

foundation.name: French
notes: There are 26 core letters. Accented letters and ç are written forms, rather than extra alphabet positions. é usually gives /e/; è and ê often give /ɛ/. ç keeps c soft before a, o or u. The letter name u is /y/: say ee with rounded lips. French ou is /u/.

ch usually gives /ʃ/; gn gives /ɲ/. an/en, on and in often mark nasal vowels when not followed by another vowel or a doubled n/m. Many final consonants are silent, but pronunciation must be learned with the word. eau often represents /o/.

An obligatory liaison occurs in les amis: /lezami/. It is normally forbidden after et and after a singular noun. The final pronounced syllable of a rhythmic group carries prominence; do not give every word an English-style stress. Learn a recording together with its written phrase.
building: un livre → le livre → les livres = a book → the book → the books. belle maison = beautiful house; plural belles maisons. Gender belongs to the noun; learn it with un/une.
de + le → du; à + le → au; de + les → des; à + les → aux. These are contractions: Je vais au marché. = I am going to the market.

possible → impossible; organiser → organisation; utile → utilement is not the usual adverb: use utilement only in suitable contexts. Learn natural collocations rather than adding suffixes to every word.

sections.title: Sound, spelling and noun phrases
sections.explanation:
French spelling is not a direct pronunciation key. Learn /y/ in tu separately from /u/ in tout; nasal vowels are not simply an oral vowel followed by a pronounced n. Liaison links a normally silent final consonant in certain contexts, but can be obligatory, optional or prohibited. Enchaînement resyllabifies a consonant that is already pronounced. Listening distinguishes them better than spelling alone.
Articles and adjectives agree with nouns. Le problème, la méthode, les résultats. Elision produces l'étude. Partitive expressions such as du café and de la patience can introduce an unspecified amount; ordinary negation commonly changes indefinite and partitive objects to de: Je n'ai pas de temps. With être and contrastive contexts, different patterns occur. Feminine singular nouns beginning with stressed /a/ are not the Spanish article system; do not import another Romance language's rule.
examples: une méthode précise / des méthodes précises
a precise method / precise methods
Gender and number agreement are visible in writing even when some endings are silent.
Je n’ai pas de réponse.
I do not have an answer.
De replaces an indefinite object article under ordinary negation.
exercises: Correct: un question important.
Une question importante. Question is feminine; article and adjective agree.
Explain tu and tout.
They contrast front rounded /y/ and back rounded /u/. English spelling cannot reliably produce the distinction.

sections.title: Verb system and past perspectives
sections.explanation:
Present forms of parler are parle, parles, parle, parlons, parlez, parlent. Many frequent verbs are irregular: être, avoir, aller and faire deserve retrieval practice. The passé composé presents past events as bounded; the imparfait commonly presents background, habit or an unfolding state. Their choice follows narrative perspective rather than a simple completed/unfinished rule.
Compound tenses use avoir or être with a past participle. With être in ordinary intransitive constructions, the participle agrees with the subject: elles sont arrivées. With avoir, preceding direct objects can trigger agreement: les lettres que j'ai écrites. Pronominal verbs need their own object analysis; do not apply a blanket subject-agreement rule. The plus-que-parfait places an event before a past reference point.
examples: Quand je suis arrivé, elle travaillait.
When I arrived, she was working.
A bounded arrival is set against an ongoing background.
Les notes que j’ai prises sont utiles.
The notes I took are useful.
Prises agrees with preceding direct object notes.
exercises: Distinguish je savais and j’ai su.
Je savais presents knowing as a state or background; j’ai su can present coming to know or a bounded knowing event in context.
Complete: Elles sont arrivé__ hier.
Elles sont arrivées hier. Feminine plural agreement with an être compound tense.

sections.title: Pronouns, y, en and relative structures
sections.explanation:
Unstressed object pronouns usually precede the conjugated verb or the infinitive they belong to. Learn the order rather than placing each pronoun from an English translation. Je le lui donne places direct object le before indirect object lui. Positive imperatives use a different pattern: donne-le-moi.
Y commonly replaces a location or an à-complement referring to a thing; en commonly replaces de + noun or a quantity expression. Human references and verb government can require other choices. Relative qui is normally a subject and que a direct object. Dont replaces a de relationship; où often relates to place or time. Lequel forms follow certain prepositions and agree with the antecedent. Distinguish the antecedent's gender from the pronoun's grammatical role.
examples: C’est une question dont nous discutons.
It is a question that we are discussing.
Discuter de licenses dont.
J’en ai lu trois.
I have read three of them.
En carries the understood noun associated with the quantity.
exercises: Combine: Voici la méthode. Nous avons besoin de cette méthode.
Voici la méthode dont nous avons besoin. Avoir besoin de licenses dont.
Replace à cette question: Je réfléchis à cette question.
J’y réfléchis. Y replaces the thing-complement governed by à.

sections.title: Subjunctive, condition and uncertainty
sections.explanation:
The subjunctive commonly appears after expressions of necessity, desire, evaluation or doubt. Il faut que vous soyez précis; je souhaite qu'elle vienne. It is not simply a tense for anything uncertain. Although an event can be factual, bien que normally takes the subjunctive: bien qu'il soit tard. Après que normally takes the indicative in standard usage, despite common variation.
Si clauses use coordinated tense patterns: si + present with a real future consequence; si + imperfect with conditional for a hypothetical situation; si + pluperfect with past conditional for a past counterfactual. Do not use the conditional automatically after si in the ordinary condition structure. Literary imperfect and pluperfect subjunctives are recognition topics for advanced reading rather than default everyday production.
examples: Bien que les résultats soient prometteurs, une confirmation reste nécessaire.
Although the results are promising, confirmation remains necessary.
Subjunctive follows bien que; the main assertion states the limitation.
Si j’avais su, j’aurais attendu.
If I had known, I would have waited.
Past counterfactual: plus-que-parfait and conditionnel passé.
exercises: Correct: Si j’aurais le temps, je viendrais.
Si j’avais le temps, je viendrais. The ordinary hypothetical condition uses imperfect after si.
Why does bien que take subjunctive even with a true fact?
Mood is governed by the construction and its concessive framing, not solely by factual uncertainty.

sections.title: Passive, causative and reported information
sections.explanation:
The passive uses être + participle, agreeing with the subject. French also uses on, reflexive constructions and active wording where English might prefer a passive. Le français se parle dans plusieurs régions uses a pronominal construction. Faire + infinitive is causative: faire réparer le vélo means arranging for the bicycle to be repaired.
Reported speech can change pronouns, time expressions and tense perspective: elle a dit qu'elle viendrait. The conditional can also mark unconfirmed information in journalistic register, as in the report-style Il y aurait plusieurs causes. This is a reporting convention, not the assertion that the writer has disproved the information. Explain the source and degree of confidence explicitly when precision matters.
examples: Le rapport a été révisé par l’équipe.
The report was revised by the team.
Compound passive with agreement on rapport.
Nous avons fait vérifier les chiffres.
We had the figures checked.
Faire + infinitive expresses arranged or caused action.
exercises: Rewrite actively: Une décision a été prise par le comité.
Le comité a pris une décision. The agent becomes clearer.
Explain elle a dit qu’elle viendrait.
She said she would come. The conditional represents a future viewed from a past reporting point.

sections.title: Argument connectors, nominalisation and register
sections.explanation:
Cependant and toutefois introduce qualifications or contrast; en revanche presents a counterbalancing contrast; par conséquent signals inference; néanmoins expresses concession. Do not scatter connectors without an actual logical relation. French academic prose often uses nominalisations, but excessive noun stacking obscures agency.
Politeness includes appropriate address: vous for many professional relationships, tu for familiar ones depending on community and context. Pourriez-vous préciser ... is a conventional request. Formal letters use established opening and closing formulas, while contemporary email can be less ceremonial. Register should match purpose, not a fixed belief that French must always sound ornate.
examples: Cette hypothèse est plausible ; toutefois, les données restent insuffisantes.
This hypothesis is plausible; however, the data remain insufficient.
The connector limits the implication of plausibility.
Pourriez-vous préciser les conditions de cette estimation ?
Could you clarify the conditions of this estimate?
Conditional politeness with a precise object.
exercises: Replace the vague Cela prouve tout with a cautious academic claim.
Ces résultats soutiennent cette interprétation, sans exclure les autres explications. The claim stays limited.
Write a request to a professional contact.
Use vous, a clear purpose and a practical next step. Avoid combining several elaborate politeness formulas in one sentence.

sections.title: Advanced reading and stylistic distinctions
sections.explanation:
Original teaching passage: Une explication peut sembler convaincante sans être confirmée par les données disponibles. Il convient donc de distinguer ce que les observations montrent de ce que l'auteur en déduit. Plus les conditions de l'étude sont clairement définies, plus il devient possible d'évaluer la portée de ses conclusions. Cette prudence ne rend pas l'analyse moins utile ; elle en précise les limites.
Translation: An explanation can appear convincing without being confirmed by the available data. It is therefore appropriate to distinguish what the observations show from what the author infers from them. The more clearly the study conditions are defined, the more possible it becomes to assess the scope of its conclusions. This caution does not make the analysis less useful; it clarifies its limits.
Convaincant concerns persuasiveness; confirmé concerns evidential confirmation. Portée refers to scope or reach, not just a literal distance. En links an inference to its source and later links limits to the analysis. Advanced reading requires tracking these small references.
examples: ce que l’auteur en déduit
what the author infers from it/them
Ce que introduces an indefinite relative; en represents the source relationship.
Il convient de distinguer ...
It is appropriate to distinguish ...
A formal impersonal recommendation rather than a command.
exercises: What does the final sentence deny?
It denies that caution makes the analysis less useful; it instead clarifies the limits.
Rewrite the passage for a friend in 80 words.
Keep the evidential distinction but simplify impersonal phrasing. Check natural register and references, not only grammar.

sections.title: Idiomatic competence and broad learning
sections.explanation:
Learn idioms as situated examples. En fin de compte means ultimately; en revanche is a contrast marker; avoir beau + infinitive expresses unsuccessful effort or a concessive idea. Avoir beau chercher, je ne trouve rien means that however much I search, I find nothing. It does not concern literal beauty. Regional lexical choices such as déjeuner and dîner can designate different meals in different Francophone regions.
For near-native ambition, read essays, quality journalism, literature, letters and specialised prose. Notice humour, understatement, formality and social positioning. Literary passé simple is central for recognition in narrative, although it is not an everyday conversational default. Maintain a phrase notebook that records an entire useful construction and its circumstances.
examples: Il a beau vérifier, il ne trouve aucune erreur.
However much he checks, he finds no error.
Avoir beau frames an effort that fails to change the result.
En fin de compte, la décision dépend du contexte.
Ultimately, the decision depends on the context.
A discourse phrase, not a literal accounting statement.
exercises: Why should you not translate every instance of beau as beautiful?
Fixed constructions can have nonliteral meanings; avoir beau + infinitive is a standard example.
Analyse a page of authentic French from any subject.
Extract three collocations, one clause structure, one register choice and an accurate summary. Check the source before treating its statements as evidence.

rules.title: Articles and gender
rules.explanation: Articles distinguish gender, number and reference. Le/la are singular definite forms and les is plural. Un/une introduce indefinite singular nouns. Learn each noun with its article; a translation rarely predicts gender.

examples.native: Il a été condamné à de la prison.
examples.translation: He was sentenced to prison.

examples.native: Il n'est qu'un homme d'affaires.
examples.translation: He is nothing but a businessman.

examples.native: C'est un très bon ami, mais il est un peu paresseux.
examples.translation: He is a very good friend, yet a little lazy.

rules.title: Contractions and partitives
rules.explanation: Du can be de + le or a partitive article. Au and aux contract à + le/les. Meaning and the governing phrase distinguish possession, source, destination and unspecified quantity.

examples.native: Roger travaille du matin au soir.
examples.translation: Roger works from morning till night.

examples.native: Cette partie du musée est temporairement inaccessible aux visiteurs.
examples.translation: This part of the museum is temporarily off-limits to visitors.

examples.native: Allez-vous au théâtre ce soir ?
examples.translation: Are you going to the theater tonight?

rules.title: Subject pronouns
rules.explanation: A finite verb normally has an expressed subject. On takes third-person singular agreement and often means people generally or informal we. Vous can address one person politely or several people.

examples.native: Tom ne semble certainement pas savoir ce qu'il est en train de faire.
examples.translation: Tom certainly doesn't seem to know what he's doing.

examples.native: Je ne pense pas que tu devrais manger ça.
examples.translation: I don't think you should eat that.

examples.native: Je n'ai pas appris cela en lisant.
examples.translation: I didn't learn this through reading.

rules.title: Present être
rules.explanation: Être is irregular: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont. It can be a main copula or an auxiliary; a later participle helps identify the latter.

examples.native: C'est chaud boulette.
examples.translation: It's as hot as toast.

examples.native: Mon stylo est à court d'encre.
examples.translation: My pen is out of ink.

examples.native: Je suis venu à Tokyo pour assister à une conférence.
examples.translation: I came to Tokyo to attend a conference.

rules.title: Present avoir
rules.explanation: Avoir expresses possession and forms many compound tenses. Some expressions use avoir where English uses be: avoir faim, avoir vingt ans. Do not translate the English verb mechanically.

examples.native: Qu'y a-t-il à faire ?
examples.translation: What's there to do?

examples.native: J'ai besoin de ton aide.
examples.translation: I need your help.

examples.native: Tom a été très respectueux.
examples.translation: Tom has been very respectful.

rules.title: Imperfect perspective
rules.explanation: The imparfait often presents a background state, ongoing situation or past habit. It does not simply mean a long event. Contrast it with a completed event in the passé composé.

examples.native: C'était une journée agréable, mais il y avait peu de monde dans le parc.
examples.translation: It was a pleasant day, but there were few people in the park.

examples.native: Aota n'était pas digne de ta confiance.
examples.translation: Aota was not worthy of your trust.

examples.native: Vos questions étaient trop directes.
examples.translation: Your questions were too direct.

rules.title: Past participles
rules.explanation: A past participle combines with avoir or être in a compound tense. Agreement depends on the auxiliary and the construction; with avoir a preceding direct object can matter. A participle may also act adjectivally.

examples.native: L'état fait face à une crise financière.
examples.translation: The state faces a financial crisis.

examples.native: Je suis en fait plutôt flattée.
examples.translation: I'm actually kind of flattered.

examples.native: Je suis venu pour vous poser une question.
examples.translation: I've come to ask you a question.

rules.title: Future forms
rules.explanation: The futur simple locates an event ahead or makes a prediction. Aller plus infinitive is another future construction. In many future-time clauses after quand, French uses future where English uses present.

examples.native: Peut-être que ce sera suffisant.
examples.translation: Maybe that'll be enough.

examples.native: Un verre d'eau vous fera du bien.
examples.translation: A glass of water will make you feel better.

examples.native: J'ignore quand il sera là.
examples.translation: I don't know when he'll be here.

rules.title: Conditional forms
rules.explanation: The conditional can express a hypothetical result, politeness or unconfirmed reported information. A usual hypothetical pattern is si + imperfect, conditional in the main clause.

examples.native: Tu ne voudrais prendre un peu l'air ?
examples.translation: Wouldn't you like to get some fresh air?

examples.native: Je ne pourrais pas me passer de ce dictionnaire, ne serait-ce que pour une journée.
examples.translation: I cannot do without this dictionary even a day.

examples.native: Tu aurais dû lui dire la vérité.
examples.translation: You should have told him the truth.

rules.title: Subjunctive contexts
rules.explanation: Subjunctive forms occur after many expressions of necessity, desire, doubt and evaluation. The governing expression matters: il faut que commonly takes a subjunctive. A form alone does not establish a speaker’s certainty.

examples.native: Ne te rappelles-tu pas quoi que ce soit ?
examples.translation: Don't you remember anything?

examples.native: Il est plus riche que qui que ce soit d'autre en ville.
examples.translation: He is richer than anybody else in town.

examples.native: Que Dieu l'ait en sa sainte miséricorde.
examples.translation: May God have mercy on him.

rules.title: Object pronouns
rules.explanation: Direct and indirect object pronouns differ. Lui/leur often replace an animate à-complement; le/la/les replace direct objects. Pronouns generally precede the finite verb, with special imperative ordering.

examples.native: Voulez-vous sortir d'ici ou non ?
examples.translation: Do you want to get out of here or not?

examples.native: Je viens te chercher.
examples.translation: I'm coming to pick you up.

examples.native: Faisons-nous l'objet d'une accusation ?
examples.translation: Are we being charged with something?

rules.title: Y and en
rules.explanation: Y often replaces a place or an à + non-person complement. En often replaces a de-complement or partitive quantity. Retain an expressed number when needed: J’en ai deux. En can also begin a different construction, so inspect context.

examples.native: Il sait comment se tenir en public.
examples.translation: He knows how to behave in public.

examples.native: On n'en est jamais certain.
examples.translation: You never know for sure.

examples.native: Je suis en léger surpoids.
examples.translation: I'm a little overweight.

rules.title: Relative clauses
rules.explanation: Qui is a relative subject; que a relative direct object; dont normally replaces a de relation; où relates place or time. Que also has other functions. Determine the role within the clause.

examples.native: Attends ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne !
examples.translation: Wait here until I come back.

examples.native: Tom semble être conscient de ce qui se passe.
examples.translation: Tom seems to be aware of what's happening.

examples.native: Où vis-tu exactement ?
examples.translation: Where exactly do you live?

rules.title: Negation
rules.explanation: Formal French commonly uses ne with pas/jamais/rien/personne/plus. Spoken French often drops ne. Plus can mean no longer in a negative construction or more in an affirmative one; pronunciation and context matter.

examples.native: Ne m'arnaquez pas !
examples.translation: Don't screw me over!

examples.native: Je n'aime pas qu'on se moque de moi.
examples.translation: I don't like being made a fool of.

examples.native: Ne dites rien à ma blonde !
examples.translation: Don't tell my girlfriend.

rules.title: Questions and indirect questions
rules.explanation: Questions can use intonation, est-ce que or inversion. An indirect question normally keeps statement order. Si introduces an indirect yes/no question as well as a condition in other contexts.

examples.native: Combien de tuyaux compte cet orgue ?
examples.translation: How many pipes does this organ have?

examples.native: Combien la chemise coûte-t-elle ?
examples.translation: How much does the shirt cost?

examples.native: Comment trouvez-vous Kyoto ?
examples.translation: How do you like Kyoto?

rules.title: Conditions
rules.explanation: Si introduces several meanings, especially if and indirect whether. For a standard unreal present condition use si + imperfect, not conditional. For a past counterfactual use si + pluperfect.

examples.native: Nous n'étions pas si occupées.
examples.translation: We weren't all that busy.

examples.native: Si j'étais vous, je ne le traduirais pas littéralement.
examples.translation: If I were you, I wouldn't translate it literally.

examples.native: Si l'on devait nommer les pays d'après les mots qu'on y entend d'abord, l'Angleterre s'appellerait “damn it”.
examples.translation: If countries were named after the words you first hear when you go there, England would have to be called Damn It.

rules.title: Cause and concession
rules.explanation: Parce que supplies a cause; puisque often treats the reason as accepted; bien que introduces concession and generally takes subjunctive. Pourtant/cependant link ideas without themselves supplying the same subordinate structure.

examples.native: Tu ne connais pas Tom aussi bien que moi.
examples.translation: You don't know Tom as well as I do.

examples.native: Je ne parle pas bien l'anglais, bien que je l'aie étudié six ans à l'école.
examples.translation: I don't speak English well even though I took it for six years at school.

examples.native: Garde tes distances parce que j'ai un mauvais rhume.
examples.translation: Keep away from me because I have a bad cold.

rules.title: Causative faire
rules.explanation: Faire can mean do/make or form a causative with an infinitive: faire réparer, have repaired. Identify who arranges the action and who performs it. Not every occurrence of faire is causative.

examples.native: Fais ton déplacement.
examples.translation: Make your move.

examples.native: N'importe quel enfant peut faire cela.
examples.translation: Any child can do that.

examples.native: J'ai envie de te faire un câlin.
examples.translation: I want to give you a hug.

rules.title: Adjective agreement
rules.explanation: Adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number, with many spelling changes. Their position can affect meaning. Written agreement is often more visible than spoken agreement.

examples.native: Est-ce ta petite copine ?
examples.translation: Is this your girlfriend?

examples.native: Ma mère m'a acheté un nouveau vélo.
examples.translation: Mother bought me a new bicycle.

examples.native: C'est de nouveau plein, aujourd'hui.
examples.translation: It's crowded again today.

rules.title: Comparison
rules.explanation: Plus/moins ... que compare; aussi ... que expresses equality. Meilleur compares bon; mieux compares bien. Choose adjective versus adverb according to the phrase’s function.

examples.native: Mon meilleur ami est mort asphyxié.
examples.translation: My best friend died of asphyxiation.

examples.native: Tom est fort, mais Marie est plus forte.
examples.translation: Tom is strong, but Mary is stronger.

examples.native: Un des plus gros problèmes dans notre société moderne, c'est que les gens ne voient pas le monde comme moi.
examples.translation: One of the biggest problems in our modern society is that the people don't see the world as I do.

passages.title: Learning with a clear purpose
passages.native: J’apprends une nouvelle langue. Chaque jour, je lis un texte court et j’écoute des exemples clairs. J’écris des mots utiles dans un cahier. Quand je fais une erreur, je vérifie la règle et j’essaie encore. Mon objectif est de comprendre les gens et d’exprimer mes idées clairement.
passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

passages.title: Philosophy: definitions and disagreement
passages.native: Deux personnes peuvent employer le même mot sans lui donner exactement le même sens. Avant de conclure qu'elles sont en désaccord, il est donc utile de préciser les termes de la discussion. Une définition ne résout pas nécessairement le problème, mais elle permet de mieux identifier ce qui reste à expliquer. Il faut également distinguer une définition proposée pour un objectif particulier d'une description de l'usage ordinaire. Dans un débat sérieux, les exemples limites sont souvent aussi instructifs que les exemples évidents, car ils révèlent les conditions que l'on avait laissées implicites.
passages.guide: People can use the same word with different meanings. Clarifying terms can reveal whether they really disagree. A definition does not necessarily solve the problem, but makes the remaining issue clearer. A purpose-specific definition differs from a description of ordinary usage. Borderline examples can reveal previously implicit conditions.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
